A few days ago, OpenAI accused Apple of improperly introducing new evidence in a trade secrets case. Today, Apple has hit back, claiming OpenAI's response overstepped what the court rules allow. Here are the specifics.

Apple argued that OpenAI's actions went beyond simply objecting to the new evidence.

In the case where Apple is suing two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products over alleged theft of trade secrets, one of the disputed points involves Apple's application for a temporary restraining order (TRO).

In short, Apple is asking the court to issue a TRO on the grounds that, while the case proceeds, doing so could prevent its trade secrets from being further embedded into OpenAI's hardware development.

In legal filings submitted by both sides, Apple filed an opposition brief along with five expert declarations. The defendants subsequently accused Apple of improperly introducing new evidence and asked the court to strike portions of the filings.

In its opposition brief, OpenAI and the other defendants did not merely claim that Apple had introduced new evidence; they went further and submitted additional filings to rebut Apple's arguments.

Apple responded today to those opposition briefs, accusing the defendants of not merely objecting to new evidence but of raising an entirely new set of arguments and evidence:

Under Local Rule 7-3(d)(1), a party may object to new evidence in an opposition brief, but the rule also specifies that the filing "must not include further arguments in support of the motion." The defendants did not respect this limit, instead using their filings to re-litigate the substance of Apple's TRO motion. For example, the defendants questioned whether Dr. Runge "had a basis for conducting any analysis," whether he had adequately addressed "contradictory evidence," and whether he could establish that certain Apple information was not publicly available. […] Such arguments are not objections to new evidence. (Saying that "some of the plaintiff's arguments lack evidentiary support or are contradicted by other evidence" is not an "objection to evidence.")

Apple also objected to a new declaration submitted by Liu, describing it as the defendants' "most egregious overreach":

Notably, when submitting Liu's declaration, the defendants said that the declaration should only be considered if the court simultaneously decided to consider the Apple evidence the defendants had challenged.

Apple argued that, since the defendants have now raised an entirely new set of arguments, the court should consider the entire record rather than striking any evidence from Apple's opposition brief.

The court is scheduled to hear Apple's TRO application on October 14.
